title: How a dead animal becomes a fossil
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why are fossils made of stone?

explain.say: Most living things rot away completely when they die. A fossil forms only when something special happens: the body is buried quickly, often in mud on a sea floor or riverbed.

explain.say: Covered by mud and sand, the body is protected from scavengers and air. The soft parts usually rot, but hard parts like bones, shells and teeth remain.

faq.q: Why are fossils made of stone?
faq.a: Water carrying dissolved minerals soaks into buried bone or wood. The minerals fill the tiny spaces and slowly replace the original material, so the shape is copied in stone.
asks: How does bone turn into rock?

faq.a: Most dead things are eaten or rot before they can be buried. A fossil needs quick burial, the right minerals and millions of years without being destroyed, so only a tiny fraction of living things ever become fossils.
asks: Why don't all animals become fossils?

faq.a: Trace fossils are signs of life rather than body parts, like footprints, burrows, nests and droppings. Dinosaur footprints are trace fossils.
To count as a fossil, something is usually at least about 10,000 years old. The oldest fossils, of microbes, are over 3 billion years old.

faq.q: Can fossils form in other ways?
faq.a: Yes. Insects can be trapped in tree resin that becomes amber, and mammoths have been frozen in ice. These keep even soft parts.

facts: Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rocks like sandstone, shale and limestone.
The oldest known fossils are microbial structures more than 3 billion years old.
